title: Redox, Group 2 and the Halogens
seo_title: Year 12 A Level Chemistry: Redox and Inorganic Chemistry Worksheets
standard_text: Oxidation states, redox reactions and half-equations, periodicity across period 3, the group 2 metals and their compounds, the halogens and halide ions, and tests for ions.
meta_desc: Free Year 12 A level chemistry worksheets on redox and inorganic chemistry: oxidation states, half-equations, period 3 trends, group 2 and group 7 reactions, and tests for ions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons.
key_sub: Oxidation states add up to the charge on the species.
body_html:
How to think about it

Assign oxidation states with simple rules: elements are 0, O is −2 (except peroxides), H is +1 (except metal hydrides), and the total equals the overall charge. An oxidising agent accepts electrons and is itself reduced.

Down group 2 reactivity and hydroxide solubility increase, while sulfate solubility decreases. Down group 7 oxidising power decreases and the halide ions become stronger reducing agents. Silver nitrate tests: Cl⁻ white, Br⁻ cream, I⁻ yellow.

Example

Oxidation state of Mn in MnO₄⁻?

4 × (−2) = −8

Mn − 8 = −1

Answer: +7

Example

Test result for bromide ions with acidified AgNO₃?

AgBr forms

Answer: cream precipitate

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the overall charge when finding oxidation states.
  • Saying oxidation is gain of electrons.
  • Mixing up the trends in solubility of group 2 hydroxides and sulfates.

items.q: Is this change oxidation or reduction: NO₃⁻ → NO (in acid)?
items.e: NO₃⁻ + 4H⁺ + 3e⁻ → NO + 2H₂O. Electrons on the left mean reduction (gain); on the right mean oxidation (loss).

items.q: Why is barium sulfate safe to use in a 'barium meal'?

items.q: Chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution. What is seen?
items.e: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine, so it displaces it: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.

items.q: What colour precipitate forms when silver nitrate is added to iodide ions?
items.e: AgI does not dissolve in ammonia.

items.q: Why is chlorine added to drinking water?
items.e: The benefit outweighs the risk from chlorinated compounds.

items.q: Bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution. What is seen?

items.q: How does electronegativity change down group 7?
items.e: The bonding pair is further from the nucleus.

items.q: What colour precipitate forms when silver nitrate is added to chloride ions?

items.q: Which silver halide dissolves in dilute ammonia?
items.e: AgBr needs concentrated ammonia; AgI does not dissolve.

items.q: Which halide ion is the strongest reducing agent?
items.e: Iodide reduces concentrated sulfuric acid all the way to H₂S.

items.q: Which reagent is used to test for halide ions?
items.e: Silver halides form coloured precipitates.

items.q: Why is the silver nitrate acidified with nitric acid in the halide test?
c: to remove carbonate ions that would also give a precipitate
items.e: Hydrochloric acid would add Cl⁻ ions.

items.q: Which product shows that iodide reduces concentrated sulfuric acid strongly?
items.e: Sulfur goes from +6 to −2.

items.q: Which ionic equation shows chlorine water reacting with potassium iodide solution?
items.e: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than iodine, so it displaces it: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂.

items.q: What colour precipitate forms when silver nitrate is added to bromide ions?
items.e: AgBr dissolves in concentrated ammonia only.

items.q: Which gas forms when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium chloride?
items.e: Cl⁻ is too weak a reducing agent to reduce H₂SO₄.

items.q: What forms when chlorine reacts with cold dilute sodium hydroxide?
items.e: Chlorine is both oxidised and reduced (disproportionation).

items.q: How does the oxidising power of the halogens change down group 7?
items.e: The atoms get bigger, so they attract an extra electron less strongly.

items.q: Which ionic equation shows chlorine water reacting with potassium bromide solution?
items.e: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine, so it displaces it: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.

items.q: What is seen when chlorine reacts with water in sunlight?
c: bubbles of oxygen form and the solution becomes colourless
items.e: 2Cl₂ + 2H₂O → 4HCl + O₂.

items.q: What is disproportionation?
c: a reaction with no electron transfer
the same element is both oxidised and reduced
items.e: For example Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO.

items.q: What colour is iodine vapour?
items.e: Solid iodine is grey-black.

items.q: How many electrons appear in the balanced half-equation for 2IO₃⁻ → I₂ (in acid)?
items.e: 2IO₃⁻ + 12H⁺ + 10e⁻ → I₂ + 6H₂O: 10 electrons.

items.e: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. Electrons on the left mean reduction (gain); on the right mean oxidation (loss).

items.q: Why does the first ionisation energy drop from phosphorus to sulfur?
c: sulfur has a pair of electrons in one 3p orbital, which repel
items.e: Paired electrons are easier to remove.

items.q: What is the oxidation state of Pb in PbO<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: Oxygen is −2 (−1 in peroxides), hydrogen +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); the total equals the charge on the species.

items.q: How many electrons appear in the balanced half-equation for Cu²⁺ → Cu?
items.e: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu: 2 electrons.

items.q: Why does sulfur (S₈) have a higher melting point than phosphorus (P₄)?
c: S₈ molecules are larger, with stronger van der Waals forces
items.e: Both are simple molecular.

items.q: Is this change oxidation or reduction: 2IO₃⁻ → I₂ (in acid)?
items.e: 2IO₃⁻ + 12H⁺ + 10e⁻ → I₂ + 6H₂O. Electrons on the left mean reduction (gain); on the right mean oxidation (loss).

items.q: What is an oxidising agent?
items.e: The oxidising agent is itself reduced.

items.q: Why does the atomic radius decrease across period 3?
c: the nuclear charge increases with similar shielding
items.e: Electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus.

items.q: How many electrons appear in the balanced half-equation for H₂O₂ → 2H₂O (in acid)?
items.e: H₂O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2H₂O: 2 electrons.

items.q: What is the oxidation state of S in SO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>?
items.e: Oxygen is −2 (−1 in peroxides), hydrogen +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); the total equals the charge on the species.

items.q: Why does aluminium conduct electricity better than sodium?
c: aluminium has more delocalised electrons per atom
items.e: Al gives three electrons per atom to the sea of electrons.

items.q: Why does argon have the lowest melting point in period 3?
c: it exists as single atoms with very weak van der Waals forces
items.e: There are no bonds between atoms.

items.q: Why is there a dip in first ionisation energy from Mg to Al?
c: aluminium's outer electron is in a higher-energy 3p sub-shell
items.e: The 3p electron is also slightly shielded by 3s.

items.q: Is this change oxidation or reduction: Cu²⁺ → Cu?
items.e: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Electrons on the left mean reduction (gain); on the right mean oxidation (loss).

items.q: How does electronegativity change across period 3?
items.e: The nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same.
